questiontext.text: What happens when you read m["x"] and the key "x" does not exist in the map?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The square brackets always make sure the key exists. If it is missing they insert it with a default value and return that value, so the map grows.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: The key is created with a default value (0 for numbers)
The program stops with an error
Nothing happens and 0 is returned without changing the map

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
map<char, int> m;
for (char c : string("banana")) {
    m[c]++;
}
for (const auto& p : m) {
    cout << p.first << p.second << " ";
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Counting gives a=3, b=1 and n=2. A map visits its keys in sorted order, so the letters come out as a, b, n.

questiontext.text:
Arrange the lines so the program prints 01 (the first size is printed before the key exists, the second after).

Drag the lines into the order the computer runs them.

order the lines
 1  [[1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The first size must run on the empty map (prints 0). Then reading m["k"] quietly creates the key, and the second size prints 1.

The correct answer:

questiontext.text:
Match each map operation with its behavior.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

m[k] = v  →  [[1]]

m.count(k)  →  [[2]]

m.at(k)  →  [[3]]

m.erase(k)  →  [[4]]

m.insert({k, v})  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These operations look similar but differ in what happens when the key is missing or already present. Knowing the difference avoids phantom keys.

The correct answer:

  • m[k] = v → Creates the key or replaces its value
  • m.count(k) → Returns 0 or 1 and changes nothing
  • m.at(k) → Throws an error if the key is missing
  • m.erase(k) → Removes the key together with its value
  • m.insert({k, v}) → Adds only if the key is new

questiontext.text:
Sort each statement: does it compile for map<string, int> m;?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

m["a"] = 1;  →  [[1]]

m[1] = 5;  →  [[2]]

m.insert({"b", 2});  →  [[1]]

m.push_back({"b", 2});  →  [[2]]

cout << m.size();  →  [[1]]

m["a"].push_back(1);  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A map has no push_back, its key type is fixed (a string key cannot be an int), and an int value has no push_back either. These statements were all tested with a real compiler.

The correct answer:

Compiles: m["a"] = 1;, m.insert({"b", 2});, cout << m.size();
Does not compile: m[1] = 5;, m.push_back({"b", 2});, m["a"].push_back(1);

questiontext.text: In what order does a for loop visit the pairs of a map?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A map keeps its keys sorted at all times, so loops always visit them in ascending key order (not by value).

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: In the order they were inserted

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
map<int, string> t = {{0, "low"}, {50, "mid"}, {90, "high"}};
for (int p : {10, 50, 95}) {
    auto it = t.upper_bound(p);
    --it;
    cout << it->second << " ";
}
cout << endl;

Assume the needed #include lines and using namespace std; are already written.

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. upper_bound(p) finds the first tier that starts after p, and stepping back gives the tier that contains p. Point 10 is in "low", 50 starts "mid", and 95 is in "high".

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text: What is the typical cost of one lookup in map and in unordered_map (n elements)?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. map is a balanced tree. unordered_map is a hash table, which is faster on average but has no ordering of its keys.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: O(log n) for map and O(1) on average for unordered_map

name.text: Q16 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Complete the program so it counts how many times each letter appears and prints the count of a (2).

Drag the correct pieces into the gaps.

main.cpp
[[1]]<char, int> freq;
for (char c : string("aab")) {
    freq[c][[2]];
}
cout << freq['a'] << endl;

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Counting needs a key-to-number container, so it is a map, and ++ raises the counter of each letter by one. A set has no values.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
map<char, int> freq;
for (char c : string("aab")) {
    freq[c]++;
}
cout << freq['a'] << endl;

questiontext.text:
Match each container with its main idea.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

map  →  [[1]]

unordered_map  →  [[2]]

multimap  →  [[3]]

pair  →  [[4]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. A map stores pairs, which is why every element has first (the key) and second (the value).

The correct answer:

  • map → Sorted unique keys, each with a value
  • unordered_map → Unique keys, no order, fast on average
  • multimap → Sorted keys that may repeat
  • pair → Two values stored together as first and second

questiontext.text:
Sort each expression: can it create a new key in the map?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

m[k] = v  →  [[1]]

m[k]++  →  [[1]]

cout << m[k]  →  [[1]]

m.count(k)  →  [[2]]

m.find(k)  →  [[2]]

m.at(k)  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Only the square brackets add a missing key. count, find and at are read-only: they report a missing key but never create it.

The correct answer:

May create a key: m[k] = v, m[k]++, cout << m[k]
Never creates a key: m.count(k), m.find(k), m.at(k)
